Figure 1: Black-box GenAI image enhancement produces visually compelling outputs y from input x (here, via prompts p1 for tone manipulation and p2 for low-light enhancement), but introduces spatial misalignment, texture distortion (faces, text), content hallucination, and resolution mismatch with respect to x. We propose a post-processing method that fuses x and y into a result z that inherits the photometric enhancements of y while preserving the structure and resolution of x.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on MIT-Adobe FiveK [36] (top rows, tone manipulation) and LOL v2 [37] (bottom rows, low-light enhancement). Image fusion baselines trained with their original objectives propagate hallucinated structures from y (e.g., distorted text and faces); photorealistic style transfer methods preserve structure but miss local stylistic effects under large brightness gaps. Our method preserves the structure of x while matching the tonal style of y.

Figure 6: Representative examples from the 40-image dataset used for prompt sensitivity analysis. Activated regions in the hallucination map indicate content mismatches between the input and GenAI output. When the GenAI output remains structurally consistent with the input, the hallucination map shows few activations, as shown in row 3, last column.

Figure 2: Overview of our method. Top: during inference, 1) optical-flow alignment warps the GenAI output y to the camera input x; 2) a global photometric alignment module (PAM: S-curve, CbCr LUT, and gamma correction) maps x to ywarp while avoiding hallucination leakage; and 3) MSCU-Net with a lightweight NAFNet refiner fuses the aligned pair into the output z. Bottom: during training, triplets (xhq,x,y) are synthesized from clean patches using color/brightness shifts, detail shifts, and synthetic hallucination.
